title: Jeremiah 33:14–26
context: Jeremiah 33:14–26 is the LORD’s promise to fulfill his good word to Israel and Judah. He will cause a righteous Branch to grow for David, who will do justice and righteousness; Judah will be saved, Jerusalem will live safely, and she will be called "The LORD our righteousness." A closely related promise appears in 23:5–6, where the name belongs to the king himself; here it is given to the city. The two passages are named here without harmonizing. The LORD then promises that David will never lack a man on the throne and the Levitical priests will never lack a man to offer sacrifices. He binds these promises to his covenant with day and night: only if that covenant could be broken could his covenant with David and the Levites fail. He answers those who say he has cast off the two families he chose, promising to reverse their captivity and have mercy. The Davidic covenant (2 Samuel 7) is shared ground for both traditions, which differ more in how they trace its fulfillment than over its certainty.

verses.text: “Behold, the days come,” says the LORD, “that I will perform that good word which I have spoken concerning the house of Israel and concerning the house of Judah.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says the days are coming when he will fulfill the good word he spoke to Israel and Judah. Arminians see God’s faithfulness to his promises, which he will keep despite the people’s failures.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s sovereign commitment to fulfill his word. Both traditions read the verse as introducing the promises about David and the Levites, and they note that it recalls 29:10.

verses.text: “In those days and at that time, I will cause a Branch of righteousness to grow up to David. He will execute justice and righteousness in the land.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says he will cause a Branch of righteousness to grow for David, who will do justice and righteousness in the land. Arminian readers see the promise of a righteous king from David’s line, which Christians see fulfilled in Jesus.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the Branch as the Messiah who fulfills the Davidic covenant. Both traditions hold this as shared ground and note the close parallel in 23:5, which is named here without harmonizing.

verses.text: In those days Judah will be saved, and Jerusalem will dwell safely. This is the name by which she will be called: The LORD our righteousness.”
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says Judah will be saved, Jerusalem will live safely, and she will be called "The LORD our righteousness." Arminians note that in 23:6 this name belongs to the king, while here it is given to the city, showing that the people share the identity of their righteous king.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the city bearing the name of the righteousness God provides. Both traditions note the difference from 23:6 without forcing a single explanation, and they hold the promise of salvation and safety as shared ground.

verses.text: For the LORD says: “David will never lack a man to sit on the throne of the house of Israel.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says David will never lack a man to sit on the throne of Israel. Arminian readers see God’s faithfulness to his promise to David in 2 Samuel 7, which Christians see fulfilled in Christ.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s covenant with David as certain. Both traditions hold the Davidic covenant as shared ground, and they note that the promise came while Zedekiah, the last king of Judah, was about to lose his throne.

verses.text: The Levitical priests won’t lack a man before me to offer burnt offerings, to burn meal offerings, and to do sacrifice continually.”
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says the Levitical priests will never lack a man to offer burnt offerings, meal offerings, and sacrifices continually. Arminians see God’s commitment to restore worship along with the kingship after the exile.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the promise to the Levites as part of God’s covenant faithfulness (compare Numbers 25:12–13). Both traditions note that Christians read this promise in light of Christ’s priesthood in Hebrews, while differing somewhat in how they trace its fulfillment.

verses.text: The LORD’s word came to Jeremiah, saying,
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD’s word comes again to Jeremiah. Arminian readers see God adding further assurance to his promises about David and the Levites, which shows his care to strengthen his people’s faith.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and read the verse as introducing a new oracle. Both traditions see the repeated formula as marking the importance of what follows.

verses.text: “The LORD says: ‘If you can break my covenant of the day and my covenant of the night, so that there will not be day and night in their time,
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says that if anyone could break his covenant with day and night so they do not come in their time, then his other covenant could also be broken. Arminians see God grounding his promise in the regularity of creation, which no one can disrupt.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s faithfulness in creation as a picture of his faithfulness in covenant. Both traditions compare 31:35–36, where the same reasoning supports God’s commitment to Israel.

verses.text: then my covenant could also be broken with David my servant, that he won’t have a son to reign on his throne; and with the Levitical priests, my ministers.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says only then could his covenant with David his servant and with the Levitical priests be broken. Arminian readers see the certainty of God’s promise to David, which stands as firm as the order of creation.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the covenant with David as unbreakable because it rests on God’s faithfulness. Both traditions hold this as shared ground, consistent with how the site treats 2 Samuel 7.

verses.text: As the army of the sky can’t be counted, and the sand of the sea can’t be measured, so I will multiply the offspring of David my servant and the Levites who minister to me.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says he will multiply the offspring of David and the Levites like the stars and the sand. Arminians see the echo of the promise to Abraham (Genesis 22:17), now applied to the royal and priestly lines.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s covenant promises linked together. Both traditions note that the language is drawn from the patriarchal promises, and they read the verse as stressing the abundance of God’s blessing.

verses.text: The LORD’s word came to Jeremiah, saying,
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD’s word comes to Jeremiah once more. Arminian readers see God responding to what the people are saying, which shows that he hears both their despair and their unbelief.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and read the verse as introducing the final oracle of the chapter. Both traditions note that God’s word answers the people’s words directly in the next verse.

verses.text: “Don’t consider what this people has spoken, saying, ‘Has the LORD cast off the two families which he chose?’ Thus they despise my people, that they should be no more a nation before them.”
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD tells Jeremiah not to regard what the people say, that the LORD has cast off the two families he chose, and so they despise his people. Arminians see God answering a despairing or mocking claim that his covenant has ended.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God refuting the claim that he has rejected his chosen people. Both traditions note that the two families are likely Israel and Judah, though some suggest David and Levi, and they hold the identification lightly.

verses.text: The LORD says: “If my covenant of day and night fails, if I have not appointed the ordinances of heaven and earth,
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says that if his covenant of day and night fails, if he has not appointed the ordinances of heaven and earth, then the next verse will follow. Arminian readers see the same argument from creation as in verse 20, used to show the certainty of God’s promise.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s ordering of creation as the guarantee of his covenant faithfulness. Both traditions read the conditional form as rhetorical, since the order of creation does not fail.

verses.text: then I will also cast away the offspring of Jacob, and of David my servant, so that I will not take of his offspring to be rulers over the offspring of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob; for I will cause their captivity to be reversed and will have mercy on them.”
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says only then would he cast away the offspring of Jacob and David, but he will reverse their captivity and have mercy on them. Arminians see God’s final word of mercy, which assures his people that he will not abandon them.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s sovereign mercy as the foundation of his people’s hope. Both traditions hold the Davidic covenant and God’s mercy to Abraham’s offspring as shared ground, while differing in how they trace its fulfillment in Christ and the church.
